narrative:
Your loan application was carefully reviewed, and unfortunately, we were unable to approve it at this time. Based on the information provided, the system predicted a 59% likelihood that the loan could pose a higher risk of repayment difficulties. This decision wasn’t based on any single factor but rather a combination of details from your financial profile.

One of the most significant concerns was the current balance in your checking account. The model flagged that your account is overdrawn (showing a negative balance), which is uncommon among approved applicants—nearly none of them had this situation. While this was the strongest factor pushing the decision toward denial, your credit history actually worked in your favor. The fact that you’ve successfully repaid all past loans at this bank helped counterbalance some of the risk, though not enough to outweigh other concerns.

The amount you requested—2,746 DM—was slightly below the average loan size for approved applicants, which actually helped your case. However, the loan term you requested (36 months) was nearly twice as long as the typical 19 months approved applicants tend to choose. Longer repayment periods can increase risk, especially when combined with other factors like your installment rate, which is higher than average. Your monthly payments would take up 4% of your disposable income, compared to the 3% that most approved applicants commit to.

On a positive note, your long-term employment (over seven years) and stable housing situation (owning your home) are strengths in your profile. However, the combination of an overdrawn account, a longer-than-average loan term, and limited savings (less than 100 DM) raised enough red flags to tip the scales toward denial.

To improve your chances in the future, focusing on rebuilding your checking account balance and reducing the requested loan term could make a meaningful difference. If possible, increasing your savings or demonstrating a lower installment rate relative to your income may also help. We encourage you to review these areas and consider reapplying when your financial situation has stabilized.
